nodes.norm_label: kafka for durable hops, http for cache lookups

nodes.label: Cross-session 'continue' Resumes from Session Log / PLAN.md
nodes.norm_label: cross-session 'continue' resumes from session log / plan.md

nodes.label: Why KEDA on only one service (LEARNING.md)
nodes.norm_label: why keda on only one service (learning.md)
nodes.rationale: agent-service is genuinely bursty and scales on Kafka consumer lag; retrieval-service and control-plane get fixed replicas because their load is steady. Autoscaling everything is cargo culting — being able to say why one service and not three is the point.

nodes.label: Why no Eureka (LEARNING.md)
nodes.rationale: Kubernetes provides service discovery natively and Compose resolves by service name, so Eureka duplicates a platform feature and is a recognized anti-pattern. Spring Cloud Netflix's Ribbon, Hystrix and Zuul are in maintenance mode, superseded by Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Resilience4j and Spring Cloud Gateway.

nodes.label: Explicitly NOT Doing: Eureka / Service Discovery
nodes.norm_label: explicitly not doing: eureka / service discovery

nodes.label: CRITIC role
nodes.rationale: Re-checks each claim against its cited source and grades it SUPPORTED / UNSUPPORTED / CONTRADICTED, persisting the matched evidence passage.

nodes.label: RESEARCHER role
nodes.rationale: Takes one sub-question, searches and reads sources via retrieval-service, writes up a finding with citations. Kafka consumer on research.subtasks.

nodes.label: WRITER role
nodes.rationale: Assembles researchers' findings into a structured report of Claims rather than prose, so the CRITIC can programmatically check whether a specific sentence is supported by a specific source.

nodes.label: Kafka Consumer Config (virtual threads, concurrency 6, max-poll)
nodes.norm_label: kafka consumer config (virtual threads, concurrency 6, max-poll)

nodes.label: retrieval-service endpoint contract (search / extract / quota)
nodes.rationale: A dumb, fast, cacheable I/O layer: it does not decide what to search for and does not reason about results, so fetching logic never has to know anything about the AI side.

nodes.label: CompletableFuture default executor pitfall
nodes.rationale: The default ForkJoinPool.commonPool is sized for CPU-bound work and is wrong for blocking IO, so an explicit executor is passed — newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor here.

nodes.label: Virtual threads: when they help
nodes.rationale: They help when blocked on IO, which is ~95% of this project's wall clock, and do nothing for CPU-bound work. synchronized blocks used to pin a virtual thread to its carrier — use ReentrantLock instead.

nodes.label: ExtractCacheKey (the label maker)
nodes.rationale: extract:v1: plus 16 hex chars. The v1 is deliberate: to invalidate every cached page at once you bump it to v2 rather than hunting down and deleting keys.

nodes.label: Hashing (the fingerprint clerk)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately lifted out of SearchService once a second class needed it, so the two cache-key recipes cannot silently drift apart. It is the one part of the extract chain that is not idle.

nodes.label: UrlNormalizer (the alias detective)
nodes.rationale: Four different-looking addresses can point at one article; without canonicalization one article gets filed under four names and fetched four times. It deliberately never strips a param merely for looking unimportant - ?page=1 and ?page=2 stay distinct.

nodes.label: Semaphore(4) in front of the sidecar (planned)
nodes.norm_label: semaphore(4) in front of the sidecar (planned)
nodes.rationale: Four permits cap in-flight extractions so a dozen simultaneous researchers cannot flatten the little Python service, which has no queue or limit of its own.

nodes.label: Wired but never called
nodes.rationale: ExtractorClient is a Spring bean alive in memory on every run with a van, an address and a route, and nobody ever hands him a parcel. ExtractCacheKey.of() is called only from its own test.

nodes.label: Cache-key correctness rule
nodes.rationale: Whatever can change the upstream answer must be inside the hashed text, and whatever cannot must be left out. freshness is included even though unwired, because wiring it later would otherwise collide two different searches on one entry; maxResults and minTier are excluded because they are applied after the cache read and would force paying twice for byte-identical data.

nodes.label: Hashing is tidiness, not correctness
nodes.rationale: SHA-256 exists only to give short, fixed-length, space-free and colon-free Redis keys. Correctness lives one step earlier, in what you feed the hasher.

nodes.label: The caller fetches, the sidecar cleans
nodes.norm_label: the caller fetches, the sidecar cleans
nodes.rationale: The sidecar never opens an outbound connection, because all web access must funnel through retrieval-service so credits and caching are counted in exactly one place. Two doors to the internet would make the counting a lie. Consequently UNREACHABLE, ROBOTS_DENIED and TOO_LARGE are only visible at fetch time, in Java.

nodes.label: UrlNormalizer documented blind spots
nodes.rationale: Ports are dropped because getPort is never read, and a percent-encoded & inside a parameter value would split wrongly because getQuery decodes before the split. Documented, not handled; non-hierarchical URIs like mailto: would NPE.

nodes.label: Recorded deviation (documented divergence from PLAN)
nodes.rationale: The repo keeps deliberate divergences from the plan in PLAN blockquotes and session notes rather than diverging silently - e.g. the search-key formula and the sidecar's two-value status vocabulary.

nodes.label: Blueprint props (built, unused)
nodes.rationale: Three empty Postgres tables, three Redpanda topics with no producer, an empty common module, and a courier plus a specialist with no work order between them.

nodes.label: common module (empty toolbox)
nodes.rationale: Exists so a shared Claim/ResearchFinding type makes a field mismatch a compile error rather than a production mystery; zero source files today. Must never get spring-boot-maven-plugin, which would repackage it and break it as a library jar.

nodes.label: Python extractor sidecar
nodes.rationale: Written in Python because trafilatura, the best boilerplate-stripping library, is a Python library. It never fetches URLs, so it physically cannot report UNREACHABLE, ROBOTS_DENIED or TOO_LARGE - those belong to Java at fetch time.

nodes.label: ExtractorClient (the unemployed courier)
nodes.rationale: Built correctly, registered as a bean, and called by absolutely nobody - the canonical example of 'wired but never called'.

nodes.label: Two RestClient beans and @Qualifier ambiguity
nodes.rationale: Adding a second bean of type RestClient retroactively breaks the existing injection point, so both consumers must name their bean on the constructor parameter. The failure is at startup, loudly, not at first use.

nodes.label: Suspicious: common/README claims a dependency nothing declares
nodes.norm_label: suspicious: common/readme claims a dependency nothing declares
nodes.rationale: common/README says the three services declare it as a dependency; reading all four poms shows no such dependency anywhere. Intent is not wiring.

nodes.label: MIN_TEXT_CHARS = 200 paywall heuristic
nodes.rationale: A successful fetch that yields almost no article is nearly always a paywall teaser, cookie wall or JS-only page. Naming it PAYWALLED rather than returning empty text stops a blank 'OK' document sailing into the pipeline and failing confusingly during fact-checking. Sharp edge: a genuine 194-character article is mislabelled.

nodes.label: Sidecar statelessness
nodes.rationale: No database, cache, files or memory of previous requests, so there is nothing to clean up and nothing to roll back after a failure - all the mess lives on the caller's side of the wall.

nodes.label: Scope note: real code vs blueprint
nodes.norm_label: scope note: real code vs blueprint
nodes.rationale: Flows 1-6 narrate only running code; the agent pipeline (planner, Kafka fan-out, RESEARCHER/WRITER/CRITIC, verified report, SSE) is pointed at as blueprint so the guide never invents unbuilt code.

nodes.label: AGENTS.md project brief (stale mirror of CLAUDE.md)
nodes.norm_label: agents.md project brief (stale mirror of claude.md)
nodes.rationale: Near-identical to CLAUDE.md but diverged: it names 'Codex Haiku' instead of Claude Haiku, lists Spring Boot 3.3.x, cuts auth/VM deploy unconditionally with no Week 5 section, and its session log stops at Session 4.

nodes.norm_label: consult graphify-out/ before answering codebase questions

nodes.norm_label: verify-then-commit loop (test, compose up, poll health, curl, log, commit)

nodes.label: Known documentation discrepancies
nodes.rationale: The live BOM pins Spring Boot 4.1.0 while narrative instruction files still say Spring Boot 3.3.x and Spring AI 1.0; treat the pom as build truth. Also flags maven.compiler.release possibly missing from the root pom, and that flyway-core alone does not trigger Flyway auto-configuration under Spring Boot 4.x.

nodes.label: redis service (redis:7, allkeys-lru)
nodes.rationale: Started with --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru; the default noeviction rejects writes at the ceiling instead of making room, which is wrong for a cache where every entry is disposable and re-fetchable.

nodes.label: searxng service (port 8080)
nodes.rationale: Owns host port 8080, which is why the three Spring apps had to be moved to 8081/8082/8083.

nodes.label: SearXNG search.formats: [html, json]
nodes.rationale: json must be added explicitly because SearXNG serves HTML by default and every programmatic call otherwise fails confusingly.

nodes.label: Shared data-shape contracts (Claim, ResearchFinding)
nodes.rationale: Data shapes only, no Spring annotations, no DB or Kafka client code — staying dumb and dependency-free is what lets every module depend on it without dragging in Spring, Kafka, or JPA transitively. Deliberately omits spring-boot-maven-plugin, which would repackage it as an unusable fat jar.

nodes.label: POST /api/v1/search decision-by-decision flow
nodes.rationale: Filter tier <= minTier first, then limit(maxResults) — order matters, because limiting before filtering wastes cap slots on results that get thrown away.

nodes.label: Fetch Hardening (timeouts, scheme allowlist, private-network block)
nodes.norm_label: fetch hardening (timeouts, scheme allowlist, private-network block)

nodes.label: Cost Bounded by Call Count, Not Dollars
nodes.norm_label: cost bounded by call count, not dollars

nodes.label: A Failed Run is Published, Never Silently Dropped
nodes.norm_label: a failed run is published, never silently dropped

nodes.label: Guardrails are Configuration, Not Code Paths
nodes.norm_label: guardrails are configuration, not code paths

nodes.label: Cache raw SearXNG results before tiering
nodes.norm_label: cache raw searxng results before tiering
nodes.rationale: Caching pre-filter means tier-table edits apply instantly and one cached query serves every maxResults/minTier combination for a single credit.

nodes.label: Monorepo over polyrepo
nodes.rationale: Polyrepo solves team decoupling; one person writing both ends of every contract has no team to decouple from, so it would just mean four clones, four CI setups, and hand-bumping a shared jar.

nodes.label: Shared common module vs schema-first contracts
nodes.norm_label: shared common module vs schema-first contracts
nodes.rationale: Deliberate coupling: Spring AI binds LLM output straight to these records so a writer/critic mismatch is a compile error. The purist alternative (JSON Schema or Protobuf on the wire) is right once independent teams ship on independent schedules. Right call for one team's release cadence, wrong the moment there are two.

nodes.label: Cache Key Deviation (dropped maxResults and minTier)
nodes.norm_label: cache key deviation (dropped maxresults and mintier)

nodes.label: SSE progress streaming
nodes.rationale: A plain HTTP connection the server keeps open and writes updates into, so the page can show '3 of 6 researchers done' without polling. Chosen over WebFlux by using webmvc/SseEmitter for consistency with the other two services.

nodes.label: Where auth lives and where it does not
nodes.norm_label: where auth lives and where it does not
nodes.rationale: The honest answer to 'how did you secure inter-service communication' is: I didn't expose them. Knowing when not to add a security layer is framed as the more senior answer.

nodes.label: Spring Security + JWT on control-plane Only
nodes.norm_label: spring security + jwt on control-plane only

nodes.label: redpanda service (Kafka API, dual listener)
nodes.rationale: Advertises internal://redpanda:29092 for in-network clients and external://localhost:9092 for host clients, so both the containers and the IDE-run JVMs can connect.

nodes.label: Database schema: runs / dag_nodes / dag_levels
nodes.rationale: dag_levels has a composite PK (run_id, level) guaranteeing one counter row per level per run; depends_on and level on dag_nodes are intentionally unused, reserved for a future where sub-question B needs A's answer.

nodes.label: Kafka topics (research.subtasks / research.findings / agent.events)
nodes.rationale: 12 / 6 / 3 partitions respectively — subtasks gets the most because it is the fan-out point where parallelism is wanted.

nodes.label: Run lifecycle (10 steps, submit to deliver)
nodes.norm_label: run lifecycle (10 steps, submit to deliver)

nodes.label: Whole-system architecture diagram (built vs planned)
nodes.rationale: Plain ASCII on purpose so it renders anywhere with no plugins; every box tagged (B) built or (P) planned so the doc stays honest about what exists.

nodes.label: Beginner-friendly project guide
nodes.rationale: Written for a non-technical reader: explains the problem, architecture, technology choices, run flow, deliberate scope cuts, and live build status as of 16 August 2026, using analogies such as the AtomicInteger being 'a tally counter kept in one person's pocket'.

nodes.label: Research Platform guide (PDF render)
nodes.rationale: PDF rendering of the beginner guide, produced via headless Chrome --print-to-pdf because macOS textutil does not support pdf as an output format.

nodes.label: Maven multi-module aggregator build
nodes.rationale: Root pom is packaging=pom, holds no code, and imports the Spring Boot BOM so children ask for libraries without naming versions.

nodes.label: Redpanda (Kafka-compatible broker)
nodes.rationale: Kafka is chosen for the orchestrator-to-researcher hops precisely because subtasks run 5-90s with high variance and a durable drop box tolerates that where a request/reply call does not. Today no Java code touches Kafka at all - no spring-kafka in any pom.

nodes.label: Check Yourself (15 questions)
nodes.rationale: Comprehension check including trace-the-path questions, with answers collapsed so the reader attempts them first.

nodes.label: Suspicious: java.version never wired to the compiler
nodes.norm_label: suspicious: java.version never wired to the compiler
nodes.rationale: Only retrieval-service sets maven.compiler.release; agent-service and control-plane declare java.version but never connect it, so the first record written in them may fail with 'records are not supported in -source 8'. The same trap already bit retrieval-service in Session 4.

nodes.label: No error handling anywhere in the search flow
nodes.norm_label: no error handling anywhere in the search flow
nodes.rationale: Neither the controller nor SearchService contains a try/catch, so every failure surfaces as a bare HTTP 500. Acceptable at this stage, but known on purpose rather than by surprise. Notable ordering effect: a negative maxResults throws only after the fetch, cache write and credit spend have already happened.

nodes.label: Crash loudly on a corrupt counter
nodes.norm_label: crash loudly on a corrupt counter
nodes.rationale: Wrapping the parse in a silent try/catch that returns 0 would quietly report full credits while over-spending; a NumberFormatException and a 500 is arguably the better behaviour.

nodes.label: Reading the gauge never burns fuel
nodes.norm_label: reading the gauge never burns fuel
nodes.rationale: remaining() stores nothing, and recordSpend() is called from exactly one place - the cache-miss branch - so the second identical search costs zero credits.

nodes.label: Docker + docker-compose (5 containers)
nodes.rationale: Port mapping, healthchecks and build-vs-pull are the three details that matter. The three Java services are deliberately NOT in the compose file - they run on the host and reach the containers over localhost.

nodes.label: Problem: search ranks, it never verifies
nodes.norm_label: problem: search ranks, it never verifies
nodes.rationale: Ranking is a popularity guess; a search engine never checks whether a sentence is true. The factory decomposes a question, researches in parallel, then re-checks every claim against the page it came from and stores the supporting passage so the report says 'here, check me'.

nodes.label: retrieval-service (port 8081)
nodes.rationale: The only built-and-working service; also the single quota boundary so all web access, credits and caching are counted in exactly one place.

nodes.label: SearXNG metasearch container
nodes.rationale: The only path to the open web for search. Exactly one setting is changed: json added to search.formats, without which SearXNG returns HTML meant for human eyes and the JSON parser chokes - a documented trap that already cost this project time.

nodes.label: Spring Boot 4.1.0 + embedded Tomcat
nodes.rationale: Three boot behaviours matter: component scan, auto-configuration from the classpath, and an embedded Tomcat so the built program IS the server with no deploy step.

nodes.label: Two ignition switches (compose up, then the Java apps)
nodes.norm_label: two ignition switches (compose up, then the java apps)
nodes.rationale: Five sealed boxes run on the machine, plus up to three Java programs standing outside them phoning in through published ports; the Java services are deliberately absent from docker-compose.

nodes.label: The Story of This Codebase (guide)
nodes.rationale: Narrative guide written for someone who can read code but wants runtime behaviour; every factual claim carries a file:line citation, gaps marked COULDN'T TRACE rather than invented. Generated 2026-08-23 against commit 6955d9f.

nodes.label: Plain-text diagrams instead of Mermaid
nodes.rationale: Sequence diagrams were originally drawn in Mermaid and replaced with code-fenced text blocks so they render inside the IDEA editor too.

nodes.label: extractor service (build: ./extractor)
nodes.rationale: The only service built from a local recipe rather than a prebuilt image; its healthcheck uses python -c urllib.request because the slim base image has no curl.

nodes.label: Semaphore(4) in Front of the Extractor Sidecar
nodes.norm_label: semaphore(4) in front of the extractor sidecar

nodes.label: Per-domain Token Bucket as Redis Lua Script
nodes.norm_label: per-domain token bucket as redis lua script

nodes.label: Atomic check-then-act in Redis via Lua
nodes.norm_label: atomic check-then-act in redis via lua
nodes.rationale: Redis is single-threaded and runs a Lua script as one indivisible unit, so the read and write cannot be split. INCR is atomic but GET+SET is not.

nodes.label: Extractor Sidecar Status Enum Deviation (OK | PAYWALLED only)
nodes.norm_label: extractor sidecar status enum deviation (ok | paywalled only)

nodes.label: Jackson 3 (tools.jackson.*)
nodes.rationale: Works invisibly for @RequestBody and responses, and explicitly for the two Redis payloads. Jackson 3 renames packages from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson, so pasted internet snippets will not compile, and its parse/write failures are unchecked so no try/catch is forced.

nodes.label: pydantic validation (HTTP 422 before our code)
nodes.rationale: FastAPI wires the check from the type hint on the handler; wrong-shaped JSON is refused with a field-by-field explanation and the handler never runs. It is the same job Jackson plus Spring do at the Java front doors.

nodes.label: content renamed to snippet at the API boundary
nodes.norm_label: content renamed to snippet at the api boundary
nodes.rationale: content is the search engine's word; snippet is ours. The public API should not inherit somebody else's vocabulary.

nodes.label: Record field names ARE the public contract
nodes.norm_label: record field names are the public contract
nodes.rationale: Renaming urls to pageUrls fails silently: Jackson finds no matching field, leaves it null, and nobody notices until the real body silently processes an empty list on every request. The compiler will happily let you do it.

nodes.label: camelCase publishedAt across the language wall
nodes.norm_label: camelcase publishedat across the language wall
nodes.rationale: Python would normally write published_at, but the reply field is camelCase on purpose so it maps onto the Java record field-for-field with zero configuration. Jackson matches case-sensitively, so renaming it would deserialize as null forever with no error - a near-miss that already happened in Session 10.

nodes.label: Documentation Tasks Must Not Touch Source Code
nodes.norm_label: documentation tasks must not touch source code

nodes.label: Coding Conventions (records, RestClient, Flyway-first, constructor injection)
nodes.norm_label: coding conventions (records, restclient, flyway-first, constructor injection)

nodes.label: Accepted Risk: Scraped Text into LLM Prompt Unfiltered
nodes.norm_label: accepted risk: scraped text into llm prompt unfiltered

nodes.label: Actuator /actuator/health
nodes.rationale: Declared in all three services, but nothing automated calls it - the Java services are not in docker-compose, so it is checked by a human or the IDE dashboard. Week 5's Kubernetes plan needs exactly this probe back.

nodes.label: Healthcheck as a Python one-liner
nodes.rationale: python:3.12-slim ships without curl, so the check uses the one tool the image definitely has. /health checks nothing deliberately - if the process is wedged it cannot answer, and the silence is the signal. There is no restart policy on any service: unhealthy is a label, not an ambulance.

nodes.label: --host 0.0.0.0 vs loopback
nodes.rationale: uvicorn defaults to 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means invisible from outside, so the port mapping would knock on a door with nobody behind it. Worst of all the healthcheck runs INSIDE the container, so the dashboard would report healthy while every external caller got connection refused.

nodes.label: Distributed vs in-process coordination
nodes.rationale: Called the project's best system-design answer: an AtomicInteger is correct within one JVM and wrong the moment there are two replicas or a restart. Coordinate across instances with a shared store that has atomic operations, never in-memory primitives.

nodes.label: Theory the project does not teach
nodes.norm_label: theory the project does not teach
nodes.rationale: Java memory model, ConcurrentHashMap internals, deadlock conditions, ReentrantLock semantics, ThreadLocal leaks, and Redis persistence must be read separately. The project gives stories, not coverage; interviews want both.

nodes.label: Docker layer caching and shared base layers
nodes.norm_label: docker layer caching and shared base layers
nodes.rationale: Each Dockerfile line produces a cached layer re-run only if its input changed; two images from the same base share those layers on disk instead of each keeping a private copy. EXPOSE is documentation only - the port mapping plus --host 0.0.0.0 are what make the port reachable.

nodes.label: Dockerfile layer ordering (requirements before code)
nodes.rationale: Installing libraries is slow and copying one Python file is instant, so copying requirements.txt first means a rebuild only re-runs pip when the library list actually changed. Flip the order and every code edit re-downloads all three libraries.

nodes.label: Internal Markdown Links Must Resolve Across Renderers
nodes.norm_label: internal markdown links must resolve across renderers

nodes.label: Fan-in mechanism (control-plane README)
nodes.rationale: An in-memory Map works right up until you restart the service or run two replicas, then the count silently resets or splits and an in-flight run hangs with no error. Postgres supplies both the atomicity and the durability instead of reinventing distributed counting badly.

nodes.label: Cache-aside as an interview story
nodes.rationale: Jackson over JDK serialization because it is portable, human-readable in redis-cli, and has no serialVersionUID landmines. Cache-aside rather than write-through because the source of truth is an external API with no write path to intercept; when Redis is down it degrades to slow-but-correct.

nodes.label: The fan-in race condition war story
nodes.norm_label: the fan-in race condition war story
nodes.rationale: Two researchers finish simultaneously, both read completed = 5 and both write 6 — either nobody sees equality or both dispatch the writer twice. UPDATE ... SET completed = completed + 1 ... RETURNING makes read and write one atomic statement so exactly one caller observes equality.

nodes.label: Immutable SHA image tags over :latest
nodes.rationale: Rollback is impossible against a moving pointer and 'what is running right now' becomes unanswerable; SHA tags make rollback one line and give a free audit trail.

nodes.label: QuotaService (the meter reader)
nodes.rationale: He reads the meter; he does not switch off the power.

nodes.label: RetrievalController (the doorman)
nodes.rationale: Every method is one line; it knows HTTP, JSON and status codes and deliberately knows nothing about caching, credits, tiers or search engines.

nodes.label: SearchService (the librarian)
nodes.rationale: Knows caching, credits, tiers and search engines and deliberately knows nothing about HTTP, so a future in-process caller could use it directly with no HTTP anywhere.

nodes.label: SourceTierResolver (the quality grader)
nodes.rationale: Lower is better: government 1, big press 2, unknown 3, blog-patterns 4. Lists live in YAML so adding a trusted site is a one-line text edit plus a restart, no Java touched.

nodes.label: Method reference (CB/CO/SE/FM table)
nodes.rationale: Every non-trivial method with called-by, calls-out, side effects and failure modes. Record accessors, the three identical mains and the Python health one-liner are skipped as trivial.

nodes.label: Suspicious: the quota is a fuel gauge, not a fuel cutoff
nodes.norm_label: suspicious: the quota is a fuel gauge, not a fuel cutoff
nodes.rationale: SearchService.search calls recordSpend on every miss but never asks remaining() first, and remaining() floors at zero, so once out of credits it calmly reports 0 forever while searches keep going. Scoped, not forgotten: real gates arrive in Week 5.

nodes.label: Records, not Lombok
nodes.rationale: Every data shape is an immutable record; plain Java now generates the constructor, accessors, equals and hashCode, so the Lombok dependency is deliberately refused.

nodes.label: Everything expires on its own (no cleanup job)
nodes.norm_label: everything expires on its own (no cleanup job)
nodes.rationale: Cache entries and the quota counter carry their own 24h TTL and failed operations wrote nothing, so there is no cron, sweeper or cleanup task at all.

nodes.label: Filter before limit (stream stage order is meaning)
nodes.norm_label: filter before limit (stream stage order is meaning)
nodes.rationale: Trimming before judging would let low-quality blogs fill every slot and then be discarded, leaving far fewer results than asked for while excellent sources sat past the cut.

nodes.label: Date-in-the-key daily reset (midnight is an illusion)
nodes.norm_label: date-in-the-key daily reset (midnight is an illusion)
nodes.rationale: No @Scheduled job exists anywhere. At 00:01 the code simply builds a different key that nothing was ever stored under, Redis returns null, and the null branch reads it as 0 spent. Yesterday's counter is orphaned, not reset. Midnight is the JVM's default time zone.

nodes.label: The quota is global, not per user
nodes.norm_label: the quota is global, not per user
nodes.rationale: The key is built from the date and nothing else because authentication is cut from weeks 1-4; per-user counting arrives in Week 5 keyed off the logged-in user.

nodes.label: Store spent, not remaining
nodes.rationale: Because the stored value counts up rather than down, raising daily-limit instantly shows more credits left without touching a single stored entry.

nodes.label: The TTL is the cleaner, not the reset
nodes.norm_label: the ttl is the cleaner, not the reset
nodes.rationale: EXPIRE exists only so orphaned counters do not pile up in memory; it re-arms on every spend, so a busy day's counter cannot expire out from under you mid-afternoon.

nodes.label: Contract-first stubbing
nodes.rationale: The stub nails the promise cheaply: callers can integrate today, routing and JSON round-tripping are proven by the real machinery, and the real body later grows underneath without the contract moving. Session 4 stubbed all three endpoints; two have since grown real bodies, this one has been open for five sessions.

nodes.label: YAML key mismatch binds null and fails at request time
nodes.norm_label: yaml key mismatch binds null and fails at request time
nodes.rationale: A tier4: vs tier4Patterns mismatch binds null and only blows up in the pattern loop when a request arrives - there is no boot-time validation. This was Session 4's real bug.

nodes.label: Migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous image
nodes.norm_label: migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous image
nodes.rationale: Flyway takes a lock on startup so concurrent starts are safe, but a rollback breaks unless changes are additive — never drop a column in the same release that stops using it.

nodes.label: OAuth2 client vs authorization server
nodes.rationale: Google issues the token and we validate it; we never store a password. Candidates routinely say 'I implemented OAuth2' meaning they added a login button — know which side of the line you're on.

nodes.label: Redis vs Kafka in the same system
nodes.norm_label: redis vs kafka in the same system
nodes.rationale: Redis holds ephemeral shared state (cache, counters, locks); Kafka carries durable work that must survive restarts. Losing Redis costs performance; losing Kafka costs research runs.

nodes.label: Semaphore vs fixed thread pool
nodes.rationale: A pool bounds threads; a semaphore bounds concurrent access to a resource. With virtual threads you have effectively unlimited threads, so the semaphore does the real work. Release in finally or the leaked permit shows up hours later as unexplained slowness.

nodes.label: Thread pool sizing and CountDownLatch harness
nodes.norm_label: thread pool sizing and countdownlatch harness
nodes.rationale: CPU-bound ~= cores, IO-bound much higher or virtual threads; the benchmark sweeps concurrency 1->12 for a real curve. CountDownLatch starts all threads simultaneously so contention rather than ramp-up is measured.

nodes.label: Thundering herd / cache stampede
nodes.rationale: If the lock winner dies, the PX expiry releases the lock and a loser becomes the next winner — which is why SETNX is never used without a TTL.

nodes.label: Hex-encoded session handoff artifact
nodes.rationale: Plain hex (base16) of a UTF-8 summary was chosen because it is reversible; a hash would be one-way and could carry no information to a reading agent.

nodes.label: Test stack: JUnit 6 resolved, Mockito unused
nodes.norm_label: test stack: junit 6 resolved, mockito unused
nodes.rationale: 17 tests across four files in retrieval-service. contextLoads looks pointless but is a wiring smoke test: @SpringBootTest boots the whole context, so it only passes if every bean was built and disambiguated. Testcontainers is the stated convention but is not in place, which is why the suite fails when Docker is down.

nodes.label: Echoing the URL back in the reply
nodes.norm_label: echoing the url back in the reply
nodes.rationale: Looks redundant but is not: the service is stateless, so a caller firing several extractions at once needs the echoed URL to match each answer to its question.

nodes.label: control-plane (port 8083, blueprint)
nodes.rationale: The only service that connects to Postgres; it will own restart-proof fan-in state.

nodes.label: Postgres 16 + pgvector, Flyway, Hibernate validate
nodes.rationale: pgvector is chosen now so nobody has to migrate later. ddl-auto=validate means never let Hibernate change the schema; the rule is migration first, entity second. All three tables exist and are empty.

nodes.label: Redis 7 (Lettuce client)
nodes.rationale: Two jobs only: the 24h search cache and the daily credit counter. Lettuce connects lazily, so a dead Redis lets the app boot fine and then fails the first request with a 500 - Redis is on the critical path, not an optional speed-up.

nodes.label: Cache stampede / thundering herd
nodes.rationale: Nothing throws and no test fails - it is pure waste. Six concurrent threads compute the same key, all miss, all fetch, all write, all spend. The cache only helps after somebody finishes.

nodes.label: Single-flight lock (planned, unbuilt)
nodes.rationale: The first thread claims a short-lived marker with Redis's atomic set-if-absent and is the only one allowed to fetch; the others wait briefly and re-read. Deliberately deferred as a hand-written exercise.

nodes.label: INCR atomicity and implicit zero
nodes.rationale: INCR treats a missing key as 0 so the first search of the day needs no create-if-absent branch, and its read-add-write cannot be split, so six simultaneous searches land on 6 rather than 1.

nodes.label: Glossary (terms, annotations, patterns)
nodes.rationale: One or two plain sentences per term plus where it shows up; blueprint-only terms are marked with a brick so readers can tell built from planned.

nodes.label: Redis allkeys-lru eviction with 256MB cap
nodes.rationale: Redis defaults to noeviction, which refuses new writes when full - wrong for a cache where every entry is disposable and re-fetchable. No volume is configured, which is acceptable for a cache and a daily counter.

nodes.label: Cache-aside pattern (hand-written)
nodes.rationale: The application itself checks and writes the cache; the project plan explicitly bans the shortcut annotation (@Cacheable) so the pattern gets hand-written once as a learning exercise.

nodes.label: Versioned key prefix (search:v1:searxng:)
nodes.rationale: Bumping v1 to v2 makes an entire generation of entries unreachable so they expire on their own - far safer than hunting down and deleting individual keys. The provider segment is hardcoded so a second provider later does not force a cache-wide bump.

nodes.label: 200KB document cap (planned)
nodes.rationale: One giant document does not just waste space - under allkeys-lru it actively evicts useful neighbours. Caps protect the cache's whole ecosystem, not just its memory ceiling.

nodes.label: 7-day extract TTL vs 24h search TTL
nodes.rationale: Search results get 24 hours because news moves; an extracted article body is far more stable, so its note can sit for seven days.

nodes.label: Eager vs lazy connection at boot
nodes.norm_label: eager vs lazy connection at boot
nodes.rationale: control-plane connects to Postgres eagerly and runs Flyway, so a dead database fails boot; retrieval-service reaches Redis lazily through Lettuce, so a dead Redis boots fine and fails the request instead.
